Across diverse backbones and benchmarks, COHERE4D substantially outperforms prior methods in human--scene alignment, metric scene and camera pose reconstruction, and global human motion estimation, adding only 4,ms/frame, enabling overall inference at up to 14 FPS.

papers.title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
papers.authors_text: Yuxuan Liu, Chongyang Du, Yuhao Zhang, Jiahe Guo, Kawai Chung, Wenbin Hu, Huihao Jing, Hongyu Luo, Qing Zong, Haochen Shi, Haoran Li, Yangqiu Song
papers.summary: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.

papers.title: ViTacLab: Physically Consistent Visuo-Tactile Simulation, Benchmarking, and Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors_text: Linjing You, Zeming Yang, Zhenhao Shen, Shengqiang Xu, Guanda Li, Wenxuan Li, Jiyu Guo, Jasper Lu, Kyle Xu, Shawn Xie, Junjie Zhu, Siyu Wu, Jian Liu, Changhao Zhang, Rongchong Li, Zeyi Li, Hengshuang Zhao, Ruihai Wu
papers.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich robotic manipulation, but existing visuo-tactile simulators trade physical fidelity for scalability, and benchmarks largely focus on two-finger grippers. We present ViTacLab, a framework comprising ViTacSim, ViTacBench, and ViTacPolicy. ViTacSim uses a tri-modal tactile primitive: a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images. Anchored to PhysX contact-solver outputs, it corrects normal inconsistency through local stiffness alignment and reconstructs tangential forces under decoupled slip-stick regimes while preserving GPU parallelism. A joint projection preserves the sparse wrench and enforces local friction cones. ViTacBench spans parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems, with tasks ranging from vision-dominant to tactile-dominant regimes. ViTacPolicy aggregates variable numbers of heterogeneous tactile inputs using spatial-pose embeddings and a Transformer, and aligns force-array and tactile-image modalities through a two-stream VQ-VAE with a shared codebook. Controlled Hertzian-reference indentation and real-sensor sliding tests reduce normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 and 1.85 N to 0.42 and 0.53 N, respectively. Throughput reaches 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS at 256 parallel environments. Simulation and real-world experiments show gains on several contact-rich tasks, while low absolute success on tactile-dominant tasks highlights the remaining difficulty of purely tactile control.

papers.title: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
papers.authors_text: Xiaokai Song, Li Zhang, Xichao Teng, Erting Pan, Yibin Ye, Kun Wang, Leqi Liu, Guangcheng Dai
papers.summary: Image noise can confound rotation and translation estimates in monocular visual navigation for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at low and moderate altitudes, where even small perturbations may cause large errors in translation direction. Inspired by angular cues in long-range visual perception, we propose rotation-only visual odometry (ROVO) for monocular aerial imagery. ROVO estimates pairwise rotations from matched images, robustly averages them over overlapping windows, and aligns consecutive windows through shared frames. By retaining only orientation in the trajectory state, it prevents uncertain landmark depth from propagating to later estimates. In trajectory simulation, sliding-window ROVO achieved a mean orientation error just 10.7% as large as that of the conventional SLAM baseline. On real flight data, ROVO achieved rotation accuracy comparable to ORB-SLAM3 and DPVO under the original Bell412 settings. With a narrower FoV or at higher flight altitude, ROVO reduced relative rotation RMSE by 19.7--69.4% compared with the next-best method in each comparison. Code and simulation tools are available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/ROVO.

papers.title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
papers.authors_text: Jing Li, Zhe Zhang, Huateng Sun, Yuhui Yang, Wanli Xue, Xu Cheng, Fan Shi, Jianhua Zhang, Qinghua Hu, Shengyong Chen
papers.summary: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.

papers.title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
papers.authors_text: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
papers.summary: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

papers.title: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
papers.authors_text: Yi Zou, Zhuang Yan, Yudong Zhang, Xu Wang, Yang Wang
papers.summary: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

papers.title: TDD: Target-Discrepancy Distillation for Underwater Image Enhancement
papers.authors_text: Zefan Feng, Zhaocheng Yu, Laibin Chang, Kui Jiang, Junjun Jiang, Xiaopeng Fan
papers.summary: Underwater degradation changes image appearance and can compromise the semantic cues used to guide enhancement. Identifying scene content alone does not explicitly specify the appearance to recover or the input-dependent changes associated with that target. We propose target-discrepancy knowledge distillation (TDD) for underwater image enhancement, which organizes guidance around these two aspects of the same restoration problem. For each degraded-reference training pair, reference features from an underwater vision-language teacher provide target-appearance supervision, while paired feature residuals describe the observation's discrepancy relative to the same target. Both representations are jointly distilled into a lightweight guidance network that predicts them from the degraded image alone; neither the teacher nor reference images are required at inference. To align their use with their supervisory roles, we introduce progressive knowledge fusion within a multi-scale enhancement network. The estimated discrepancy first conditions spatial feature updates, after which target-appearance guidance refines the updated features and channel interactions consolidate their responses. This correction-before-refinement design lets target-guided refinement build on discrepancy-conditioned features. Experiments on six underwater benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance across full-reference and no-reference metrics. Ablations and feature visualizations analyze the contributions of the knowledge source, joint distillation, and progressive fusion.

papers.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
papers.authors_text: Kurt Horvath, Tom Tucek
papers.summary: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

papers.title: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
papers.authors_text: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.

papers.title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
papers.authors_text: Yifan Dai, Daili Hua, Bohan Zeng, Yuran Wang, Jialing Liu, Bozhou Li, Chengzhuo Tong, Yang Shi, Kai Zeng, Liu Yang, Xinyu Liu, Shujie Li, Yiyan Ji, Bingyin Mei, Yushuo Guan, Yuanxing Zhang, Fangcheng Fu, Wentao Zhang
papers.summary: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

papers.title: ViDM: Efficient and Order-Robust Parallel Visual Decision Making
papers.authors_text: Xudong Tan, Peng Ye, Chenyu Huang, Yaoxin Yang, Huafeng Qin, Tao Chen
papers.summary: Visual decision-making demands accurate judgments and timely responses. Yet for multiple questions sharing the same visual input, autoregressive multimodal large language models generate answers token by token, accumulating sequential decoding costs as question count grows and delaying completion of the decision set. Their predictions can also vary with question order. We introduce ViDM, which transforms multi-question visual inference into parallel decisions in a single forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference efficiency. ViDM organizes shared visual context, multiple questions, and question-specific decision slots into one sequence, reusing the native language-model head to produce all answer distributions simultaneously. A Decision-Query Mask aligns each decision query's direct attention with shared context and its corresponding question, while case-balanced multi-order training strengthens robustness to question reordering. Across nine benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks, ViDM improves Qwen3.5-4B's average accuracy from 73.49% to 77.55% while achieving 8.4x the baseline's average end-to-end throughput. On GQA, where each evaluated image has 11.4 questions on average, the end-to-end speedup reaches 20.3x. ViDM also improves mean and worst-order accuracy while reducing order-induced variation across multiple benchmarks, with further validation on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and InternVL3.5-4B.

papers.title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
papers.authors_text: Linghua Zhang
papers.summary: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.

papers.title: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening
papers.authors_text: Jin-Liang Xiao, Liang-Jian Deng, Yu-Xuan Zhang, Hua Meng, Zhengchun Zhou
papers.summary: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.

papers.title: ObsBridge: Observation-Grounded Conditioning for Ego Trajectory Prediction
papers.authors_text: Zhenhao Wang, Shaofeng Liang, Jiemin Wu, Sijia Chen, Keni Shi, Nan Li, Wenshuo Chen, Bowen Tian, Runwei Guan, Yutao Yue
papers.summary: Pedestrian forecasting from ego-view observations is challenging because occlusion, limited visibility, and tracking errors corrupt observed motion histories. Such errors are particularly consequential for autonomous robot navigation. Existing paradigms typically either impute noisy history positions before forecasting or jointly train an auxiliary history reconstruction branch. However, predictors trained on clean histories may be sensitive to residual errors in recovered histories at deployment. Meanwhile, auxiliary reconstruction still computes inter-agent interactions over raw, corrupted coordinates. We investigate conditioning future prediction on both recovered historical states and raw observation evidence, with progressive training to accommodate imperfect recovery. Building on this insight, we propose ObsBridge, a flow-based trajectory forecasting framework with observation-grounded historical bridging. Specifically, ObsBridge first employs a frozen estimator to recover historical motion from agent-relative and ego-relative positions, image-plane locations, and visibility states. During training, we introduce an agent-wise curriculum that gradually replaces clean teacher histories with complete estimated histories before context encoding. This progressively exposes the predictor to estimated histories during training. Furthermore, we design a residual geometry adapter to fuse the encoded motion with original observation evidence. We aggregate the resulting representations through social attention to condition the flow-based trajectory generator. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ObsBridge outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On EgoTraj-TBD, it reduces minADE@20 by 6.5\% and minFDE@20 by 8.7\%. The code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/ObsBridge.

papers.title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
papers.authors_text: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katarína Tóthová, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taixé, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
papers.summary: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

papers.title: PVWander: 3D Memory-guided Panoramic Video Wandering with Path-Facing Canonicalization
papers.authors_text: Chuanxin Song, Xiaodong Wang, Shijie Chen, Junliang Xie, Zhanmi Zhong, Suiying Wu, Peixi Peng
papers.summary: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.

papers.title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
papers.authors_text: Yoonki Cho, Youngju Na, Taegeun Yang, Jinhwan Seo, Sung-Eui Yoon
papers.summary: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

papers.title: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
papers.authors_text: Kian Izadpanah, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Daniel Cohen-Or, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Andreas Aristidou
papers.summary: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

papers.title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
papers.authors_text: Chenrui Fan, Qiyang Hu, Luca Scharr, Paolo Favaro
papers.summary: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.

papers.title: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
papers.authors_text: Daniel Pröll, Sebastian Hegenbart
papers.summary: Defect-free industrial samples can vary considerably in appearance, texture, and geometry. In few-shot anomaly detection, this variability has to be modeled from only a handful of images. SubspaceAD showed that a single principal subspace of foundation-model patch features is a strong training-free model of nominal appearance. However, a single subspace has to cover all of the nominal data's variability, so a deviation that is anomalous for one semantic region can be within the nominal variability of another. We propose LocalSubspaceAD, which extends SubspaceAD from a single subspace to a mixture of subspaces, assigning each group of patches with similar features its own subspace. The set of patch-features is partitioned using k-means, one subspace is fit per cluster, and each patch is scored by the minimum of re-projection residuals over all subspaces. The proposed method requires no training and no EM refinement. On MVTec AD, VisA and Real-IAD with 1, 2 and 4 shots, it improves over a single subspace (SubspaceAD) on both evaluated backbones: by 1.2 to 1.8 points image AUROC on DINOv2, and by 1.4 to 4.4 points in image AUROC, pixel AUPR and AUPRO on DINOv3. The gains are most pronounced on objects with heterogeneous nominal appearance, such as multi-instance categories and PCBs. Ablations show that the gains stem from a finer-grained model of variability through locally oriented subspaces, rather than from the subspace offsets (cluster means). We further show that the gains do not stem from added capacity alone: the local subspaces appear to capture the structure of coherent clusters in feature space, and the model does not merely act as a compressed memory bank.

papers.title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
papers.authors_text: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
papers.summary: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

papers.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
papers.authors_text: Ruiqi Zhao
papers.summary: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

papers.title: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression
papers.authors_text: Shun Kaneko, Shunnosuke Yoshimura, Akihiro Miki, Kento Kawaharazuka, Kei Okada
papers.summary: Facial robots require many coordinated, smallamplitude motions, but accommodating these motions in a compact face remains difficult. This paper presents an anatomically inspired facial-robot platform that reproduces the layered organization of the human facial musculoskeletal system. The platform comprises bone, muscle, and skin components whose geometry, shape, and attachment locations are derived from three-dimensional anatomical data. Wire-driven, compliant muscle components are routed through PTFE tubes, allowing actuation to be placed away from the face. We describe the selection and fabrication of 65 muscles (34 muscle types) required to reproduce the 47 target action units (AUs) in the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). We then evaluate the reproducibility of individual AUs in two stages: muscle actuation without skin and actuation after the silicone skin is attached. Forty of the 47 target AUs were reproduced with the muscle components, and 30 were reproduced after skin attachment. These results demonstrate the feasibility of reproducing a broad range of FACS facial expressions using an anatomically inspired musculoskeletal structure. The proposed platform provides a foundation for the systematic development and evaluation of future anatomically inspired facial robots

papers.title: TESS: Query-Guided Temporal Event-Structured Frame Selection for Long-Video Understanding
papers.authors_text: Qi Lu, Shiyan Tong, Shujie Li, Sen Li, Likun shi, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Yao Hu
papers.summary: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.

papers.title: Delay-Tolerant Formation Tracking for Multi-AGV Systems via Reference-Shift Coupling
papers.authors_text: Yunfei Bi
papers.summary: Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that transport a load together must keep a formation while each vehicle tracks its own reference, and they coordinate over wireless links with link-dependent, time-varying and jumping delays. We propose a cascade design for differential-drive AGVs modelled as kinematic unicycles: delayed data from the neighbours drive only a second-order filter that shifts each vehicle's own reference, and an unmodified gain-scheduled tracking law follows the shifted reference. A saturation keeps the shifted reference feasible, and the feed-forward is exact, so the tracking loop never sees the network. We prove that tracking and formation errors remain bounded for arbitrary delays and converge for every bounded delay and every directed, possibly switching, graph. We also construct a strict Lyapunov function with explicit constants and prove exponential convergence and a local input-to-state estimate with delay-independent gains. On undirected graphs, the coupling attenuates the formation error caused by persistent local errors by at least the factor lambda/(lambda+Lambda*lambda_2(L)) (leak lambda, coupling gain Lambda, algebraic connectivity lambda_2(L)), for any delay. Every inequality is verified with an event-driven, error-controlled simulation. A robustness study on a high-fidelity AGV model (drive dynamics, slip, localisation errors, clock offsets, lossy Wi-Fi) comprises 4,894 runs, including paired comparisons against tuned baselines. The cascade never failed, with latencies up to 4 s, 90% packet loss and up to 12 vehicles, whereas a direct delayed coupling failed when its gain saturated the drives. Coupling reduced the formation error after traction losses by 21-32% and after safety stops by up to 47%, at the price of tracking accuracy. Localisation bias and clock offsets, which no coupling law can observe, limit the achievable accuracy.

papers.title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
papers.authors_text: Jyotirmoy Nath, Neeraj Kumar, Brejesh Lall
papers.summary: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
papers.authors_text: Anirban Ray, Florian Jug
papers.summary: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

papers.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
papers.authors_text: Yuisei Iwata, Yutaka Masuda, Tohru Ishihara
papers.summary: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

papers.title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
papers.authors_text: Alessio Micheli, Alejandro Moreo, Marco Podda, Fabrizio Sebastiani, Domenico Tortorella
papers.summary: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.

papers.title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
papers.authors_text: Azhar Akhmetova, Edward Eichhorn, Boris Landa, Dmitry Kobak, Sebastian Damrich
papers.summary: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.

papers.title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.authors_text: Jiewen Hou, Guanxiang Qi, Meina Kan, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen
papers.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

papers.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
papers.authors_text: Omar Emara, Nan Lu, Dima Damen, Hazel Doughty
papers.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

papers.title: PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction
papers.authors_text: Junho Kim, Hyunyoung Choi, Jiseok Kim, Seongwon Lee
papers.summary: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.

papers.title: Adaptive and Detection-Aware Super-Resolution for Small Object Detection
papers.authors_text: Cezica-Elena Luncanu, Stelian Spînu
papers.summary: Image super-resolution aims to reconstruct a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input and is relevant for surveillance, satellite imagery, medical imaging, and object detection. This paper investigates SRCNN-based single-image super-resolution for a scale factor of x4, starting from a classical baseline and progressively introducing residual learning, Charbonnier loss, and adaptive loss functions. The proposed approach includes a three-region adaptive loss, where image areas are divided into smooth, texture, and edge regions using gradient information. The models are evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and EdgeMAE in order to measure both reconstruction quality and structural detail preservation. In addition to reconstruction evaluation, the paper analyzes the impact of super-resolution on object detection. A YOLOv8 detector is applied to images processed through bicubic interpolation and SRCNN-based variants, using images from the COCO validation dataset. The results show that improved reconstruction quality does not always lead to better detection performance. However, for small objects, a detection-aware variant combined with residual scaling improves the F1 score compared to the bicubic baseline. These results highlight the importance of task-aware evaluation when super-resolution is used in computer vision pipelines.

papers.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
papers.authors_text: Volkan Dagli, Zerrin Dagli, Daghan Dagli
papers.summary: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).

papers.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
papers.authors_text: Philomène Letzelter, Violaine Courrier, Sandrine Katsahian, Agathe Guilloux
papers.summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.

papers.title: Evolve to Learn: Gradient-aligned experience evolution for model self-improvement
papers.authors_text: Haoyuan Li, Gangyi Zhang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu, Daoxuan Liu, Jiancan Wu, Shiu-hong Kao, Wu Liu, Yicong Li, Yongdong Zhang
papers.summary: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.

papers.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
papers.authors_text: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu
papers.summary: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

papers.title: Improving Character Identity Consistency in Diffusion-Based Visual Story Generation through Identity Memory and Automatic Reranking
papers.authors_text: Maria-Emilia Grigore, Stelian Spînu
papers.summary: Automatic visual story generation using diffusion-based models has become an increasingly important research direction in generative artificial intelligence. However, maintaining character identity consistency across consecutive frames remains an open challenge, as existing models often produce significant variations in facial traits, clothing, visual style, or anatomical proportions. This paper proposes a modular pipeline to improve character identity consistency in multi-frame visual story generation using Stable Diffusion XL alongside additional conditioning and automatic selection mechanisms. The proposed system integrates LoRA fine-tuning for character personalization, ControlNet for pose-based structural control, and IP-Adapter for visual identity transfer. Furthermore, a reranking mechanism based on Best-of-K candidate selection and persistent identity memory is introduced to automatically select the most visually consistent generated images. The work also includes integrating and extending the StoryDiffusion framework into a reproducible local workflow, along with improvements for generated frame selection. Performance evaluation uses automatic metrics such as CLIP image similarity, DINO similarity, and CLIP text-image alignment. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a custom benchmark of multiple characters and visual stories organized into difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult). Both progressive variants of the proposed pipeline and extended versions of StoryDiffusion were evaluated, including SDXL baseline, Best-of-K, Identity Memory, and the Full Pipeline. Results show that reranking, identity memory, and visual conditioning reduce identity drift across frames and improve the overall coherence and stability of generated visual stories.

papers.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
papers.authors_text: Barnabas Juhasz, Rolf Pfister
papers.summary: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.

papers.title: The Activity Geometry of Discrete Generative Sampling
papers.authors_text: Xinlong Guo, Jie Zhang, Lingyou Zhou
papers.summary: Iterative refinement is a key capability of diffusion-based generation and has motivated growing efforts to bring similar behavior to discrete diffusion and flow models. A growing line of work enables such refinement by allowing previously generated tokens to be revised during sampling, thereby shaping the coupling between successive sampling states. Despite its growing role in sampler design, this coupling freedom remains insufficiently characterized. We introduce Activity Geometry to study these finite-step couplings through expected transition cost, which we call activity. We show that activity decomposes into the minimum required by the induced marginal transport and an excess term arising from the coupling. Using this minimum as a reference, we propose Minimal-Activity Finite-Time Coupling (MAFTC) to realize prescribed marginals with minimum activity without retraining or additional model evaluations. In the continuous-time limit, the minimum activity per unit time converges to the minimum expected jump rate compatible with the prescribed path. For metric-induced Gibbs paths, we further show that the activity of the kinetic-optimal flux admits a geometric decomposition. We find that total activity alone can obscure coupling excess: a sampler may approach the minimum activity required by the prescribed marginal transport while still retaining substantial coupling excess. In language generation, as the number of model evaluations increases, refinement-based samplers accumulate additional trajectory activity with limited diversity gains, whereas MAFTC reduces trajectory activity while maintaining comparable generation quality and higher lexical diversity.

papers.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
papers.authors_text: Mateen Ahmed Abbasi, Petri Ihantola, Tommi Mikkonen, Niko Mäkitalo
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing of Learned Spatial Surrogates for Transit Accessibility
papers.authors_text: Till Zacher, Markus Lienkamp
papers.summary: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.

papers.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
papers.authors_text: Jan Rohleff, Johannes Schropp
papers.summary: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

papers.title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
papers.authors_text: Manel Gil-Sorribes, Isaac Filella-Merce, Alexis Molina
papers.summary: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.

papers.title: Visual-State Graph Memory for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.authors_text: Ailar Mahdizadeh, Pritam Sarkar, Xiangteng He, Leonid Sigal
papers.summary: In streaming video understanding, the evidence needed to answer a question may have already left the recent-frame window. Keeping all frames does not scale with video length, while dropping older frames limits the model's ability to reason about the past. We propose Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory that stores the state of a stream rather than the raw sequence of frames. VSG represents the stream as a graph of objects and their relations, together with a log of events; similar to a dynamically evolving scene graph. An object observed repeatedly is represented by one persistent node, with a timestamped history of how its state changes. To determine whether a newly mentioned object already exists in the graph, we compare the relations it takes part in with those of stored objects. We build this memory as the video arrives, before the questions are known. When a question arrives, we retrieve relevant objects and events alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget. Our evaluation spans four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Under matched input budgets, VSG improves reasoning about the past while preserving real-time understanding.

papers.title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows
papers.authors_text: Zhikai Cheng, Shuanghu Wang, Li Jiang
papers.summary: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. Across four software tasks, 480 valid runs comprise 470 completions and ten request-limit endpoints. Jev full routing achieves the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, completing all 40 specialist-controlled runs along the shortest trajectory. On the initial task, mean cost falls by 49.6% (95% paired-bootstrap interval: 42.9% to 56.3%) and elapsed time by 33.2% (19.6% to 46.7%). Across three further tasks, cost reductions are 40.5% to 42.9% and concurrent elapsed-time reductions are 12.9% to 14.4%. Existence-only specialization saves just 1.8% on the initial task. Separately, Sol and Jev each select accepted actions on 100/100 reviewed retail states, with Jev using 97.88% less reference cost and 72.30% less mean request time. The results identify two requirements for efficient agent control: inexpensive decisions and trajectories that preserve those savings.

papers.title: Sub-Riemannian structure for Oriented Point Clouds
papers.authors_text: Thomas Besnier, Stefan Sommer
papers.summary: Many frameworks dealing with 3D (oriented) point clouds define locality in the ambient Euclidean space: $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs and radius balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are critical to define which points are "close to one another" and should exchange information.
